extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety managers, heat safety coordinators, occupational safety professionals, and stakeholders submitting comments on the OSHA NPRM
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the proposed OSHA heat illness and injury prevention standard requirements (training, emergency response, recordkeeping, acclimatization, employee participation, cost allocation) intended to guide employer implementation and public comment on the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: signs and symptoms of heat-related illness
rubrics_metrics.description: As defined in proposed paragraph (b), 'signs and symptoms of heat-related illness means the physiological manifestations of a heat-related illness and includes headache, nausea, weakness, dizziness, elevated body temperature, muscle cramps, and muscle pain or spasms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must train employees to identify these signs and symptoms in themselves and coworkers and when to employ the employer's emergency response procedures under paragraph (g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: signs and symptoms of a heat emergency
rubrics_metrics.description: As defined in proposed paragraph (b), 'signs and symptoms of a heat emergency means the physiological manifestations of a heat-related illness that requires emergency response and includes loss of consciousness (i.e., fainting, collapse) with excessive body temperature, which may or may not be accompanied by vertigo, nausea, headache, cerebral dysfunction, or bizarre behavior.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also may include staggering, vomiting, acting irrationally or disoriented, having convulsions, and (even after resting) having an elevated heart rate. Employers must train identification and emergency procedures for these signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer immediate actions during a heat emergency (cooling requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (g)(3)(i) would require employers to take immediate actions to reduce the employee's body temperature before emergency medical services arrive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid cooling is essential because organ damage and death risk rise quickly. Employers must be prepared to perform rapid cooling with methods practical for the work site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted/identified cooling methods and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA discusses fastest and practical cooling methods: immersion in ice/cold water (fastest), strategically placed 'ice sheets' (bed sheets soaked in ice water), dousing with cold water plus rubbing ice bags over major muscle groups, and tarp-assisted cooling oscillation (TACO) involving wrapping in a tarp with ice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA recognizes full immersion may not be available onsite; employers should use practical methods similar to those reported effective. Evidence cited: Belval et al. 2018; McDermott et al. 2009a/b; DeGroot et al. 2023; Luhring et al. 2016.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact emergency medical services immediately
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (g)(3)(ii) would require employers to contact emergency medical services immediately for employees experiencing signs and symptoms of a heat emergency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt EMS contact is critical because some heat-related illnesses can quickly become fatal; survival depends on how quickly effective cooling and EMS are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employers must perform specified aid activities until EMS arrives
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (g)(3)(iii) would require employers to also perform the activities described in paragraphs (g)(2)(i) through (iv) to aid an employee during a heat emergency until emergency medical services arrive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The employer's emergency response plan must specify these activities; training should cover how to implement them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial training required prior to work at/above initial heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1) requires employers to ensure each exposed employee 'receives, and understands, training on the topics outlined in proposed paragraphs (h)(1)(i) through (xvi) prior to the employee performing any work at or above the initial heat trigger.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures employees have necessary knowledge before exposure. Training must include comprehension measures (e.g., knowledge checks) though OSHA does not mandate specific testing forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training comprehension expectation (no mandated testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA does not mandate testing or specific modes of ascertaining employee understanding, but expects all required training will include some measure of comprehension (e.g., written/oral assessment, discussions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers should implement comprehension checks, especially for online training, and may use knowledge checks or post-training discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: heat stress hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1)(i) requires training on heat stress hazards: environmental factors (high humidity, temperature, solar radiation, lack of air movement, process heat), use of PPE/clothing that inhibits cooling, and body's metabolic heat from exertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers should make employees aware of all workplace heat sources contributing to heat stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: heat-related injuries and illnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1)(ii) requires training on heat-related injuries and illnesses, examples include heat stroke, heat exhaustion, heat cramps, heat syncope, and rhabdomyolysis, and heat-related injuries (slips, trips, falls) that may result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to Section IV Health Effects for further discussion; training should explain health outcomes and injury risks linked to heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: risk factors for heat-related injury or illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1)(iii) requires training on risk factors including physical exertion, clothing/PPE, lack of acclimatization, and personal risk factors (age, health, alcohol consumption, use of certain medications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers should explain how these factors increase heat load and affect risk; additional materials on acclimatization and personal risk factors are referenced in other sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: signs/symptoms and which require emergency action
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1)(iv) requires training on signs and symptoms of heat-related illness and which ones require immediate emergency action (see definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees must be trained to identify these in themselves and coworkers and to follow employer emergency response procedures in paragraph (g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: removing PPE, rest breaks (paid), drinking water
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraphs (h)(1)(v)–(vii) require training on importance of removing PPE that impairs cooling during rest breaks, taking rest breaks to prevent heat-related illness or injury and that rest breaks are paid, and drinking water to prevent heat-related illness or injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains rationale: removing PPE allows faster cooling; drinking adequate water and rest breaks reduce heat strain; training can address misperceptions (e.g., that cold water is harmful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: locations of break areas and employer-provided water
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraphs (h)(1)(viii)–(ix) require training on where break areas and employer-provided water are located.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures employees know where to go to utilize protections effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: importance of reporting signs/symptoms and emergency procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1)(x) requires training on reporting signs and symptoms observed personally or in coworkers and when to employ employer's emergency response procedures per paragraph (g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages early reporting to identify incidents before they escalate and reinforces procedures in the HIIPP.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: policies and procedures in the HIIPP and duty-specific tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1)(xi) requires training on all policies and procedures applicable to the employee's duties as indicated in the work site's Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Plan (HIIPP). Training may be tailored to employee duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: buddy observers need training on reporting procedures; designated emergency responders need more detailed emergency response training; employees wearing vapor-impermeable clothing need specific protections under paragraph (c)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: identity and contact information of heat safety coordinator
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1)(xii) requires employers to train employees on the identity of the heat safety coordinator, who is designated to implement and monitor the HIIPP and has authority to ensure compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers should provide name and contact information so employees can ask questions, provide feedback, or report deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: requirements of the proposed standard and employee rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1)(xiii) requires training on the requirements of the standard (including employee participation roles, no-cost implementation under paragraph (j)), and proposed paragraph (h)(1)(xv) requires training on employees' rights and anti-retaliation protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees must be informed of protections (rest breaks, water) and that employers are prohibited from discharging or discriminating for exercising rights under the OSH Act (section 11(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: access to the work site's HIIPP
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1)(xiv) requires training on how to access the work site's HIIPP, including both digital and physical copies if relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures employees can review the plan and understand policies/procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training topic: procedures for working in excessively high heat areas and warning signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(1)(xvi) requires training on procedures to follow when working in areas where warning signs for excessively high heat are required (per paragraph (f)(5)), including any required PPE and reminders to remove PPE during breaks and access rest areas and water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailors instruction to hazards of marked areas and reinforces access to protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisor and heat safety coordinator training (additional duties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(2) requires supervisors and heat safety coordinators to receive training on the topics in (h)(1) plus (h)(2)(i) policies/procedures for compliance (including monitoring plans) and (h)(2)(ii) procedures to follow if an employee exhibits signs/symptoms of heat-related illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures supervisors/coordinators can implement monitoring, respond to incidents, and perform duties specified by the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual refresher training and timing for outdoor workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(3) requires annual refresher training for employees, supervisors, and heat safety coordinators on the relevant topics; for outdoor employees the annual refresher must occur before or at the start of the heat season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA intends flexibility: employers determine heat season reasonably (often no sooner than 30 days before start); employers should time training to ensure recall and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triggers for supplemental training
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(4) requires prompt supplemental training when: (i) changes occur that affect an employee's exposure to heat at work (new tasks, relocation, heat waves, new heat sources, new PPE); (ii) changes occur in policies/procedures in (h)(1)(xi); (iii) indication an employee has not retained necessary understanding or is failing to follow policies; (iv) a heat-related injury/illness occurs at the work site resulting in death, days away from work, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental training need not repeat all initial training—may focus on new or deficient topics; 'lessons learned' or 'alert' trainings are appropriate after incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training language, literacy level, and opportunity for Q&A
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(5) requires that all training be provided in a language and at a literacy level each employee, supervisor, and heat safety coordinator understands, and that employers provide an opportunity for questions and answers about the training materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must accommodate varying educational levels and language skills (e.g., provide Spanish materials if employees do not understand English). Employers need not provide training in an employee's preferred language if the employee understands the language used. If a trainer is not present, provide contact info so employees can ask questions; employers should respond promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted training delivery modes (flexible)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA does not specify how training is delivered; acceptable methods include in-person (classroom or informal discussions), virtual (videoconference, recorded video, online training), written materials, or any combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regardless of medium, employers must ensure opportunity for Q&A and comprehension measures; online training may need additional assessment to ensure participation and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping: on-site temperature measurements for indoor work areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (i) requires certain employers with indoor work areas (where there is a reasonable expectation employees are or may be exposed to heat at or above the initial heat trigger) to create and maintain written or electronic records of on-site temperature measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records must be retained for a minimum of six months. The requirement applies only to indoor areas because outdoor temperatures can be predicted via forecasts and historical records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record retention duration and practical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA has preliminarily determined six months is appropriate (maximum time permitted for an OSHA investigation, 29 U.S.C. 658(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers can use monitoring devices that maintain electronic logs for six months or create written records if devices lack digital storage. Records help OSHA verify compliance and help employers identify trends or conditions after an incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: No cost to employees (employer bears all implementation costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (j) provides that implementation of all requirements of the standard must be at no cost to employees, including paying employees their normal rate of pay when compliance requires employee time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs include direct monetary expenses and time/other expenses to perform tasks and training. This applies across the standard (training time, access to water/shade, time to drink water, time to participate in HIIPP development, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer must cover expenses and pay employees for participation in HIIPP development/monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraphs (c)(6) and (7) and (d)(3)(iv) would require employers to seek input/involvement of non-managerial employees and their representatives in HIIPP development, implementation, reviews/updates, and in identifying areas for monitoring, and to cover expenses (e.g., travel) and pay employees their normal rate for time spent participating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer payment ensures participation is not contingent on employee ability to pay and encourages meaningful involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water provision standard (quantity, accessibility, temperature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (e)(2) would require employers to provide access to potable water for drinking placed in locations readily accessible to the employee, suitably cool, and of sufficient quantity to provide access to 1 quart of drinking water per employee per hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employer must pay for water, containers, cups/bottles, and must pay employees their normal rate for time necessary to travel to and from water and consume it if that time is required for compliance (e.g., when water cannot be provided onsite for safety reasons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization protocol for new and returning employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (e)(7) would require employers to implement an acclimatization protocol for new and returning employees exposed to heat at or above the initial heat trigger, except when employer can demonstrate the employee consistently worked under the same or similar conditions within the prior 14 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For new employees, the employer may choose either (A) implement an acclimatization plan that at minimum includes measures in proposed paragraph (f) (rest breaks, observation for signs/symptoms, hazard alert, warning signs) or (B) gradual acclimatization restricting exposure to no more than 20% of a normal shift on day 1, 40% day 2, 60% day 3, and 80% day 4. Proposed paragraph (e)(7)(ii) specifies similar protocol for returning employees (away >14 days).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of recordkeeping and monitoring to indoor vs outdoor areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (i) applies to indoor work areas only because employers cannot rely on weather forecasting to predict and monitor temperatures indoors and cannot recreate historic indoor records absent on-site measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers with indoor areas at or above initial heat trigger must conduct on-site measurements and retain records; outdoor monitoring relies on weather forecasts and is treated differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental training for failure to retain or follow procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(4)(iii) requires supplemental training when there is an indication an employee(s) has not retained necessary understanding (e.g., forgetting signs/symptoms or how to respond) or has failed to follow heat policies/procedures or comply with the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental training must be provided promptly to those employees demonstrating lack of understanding or noncompliance; may be targeted rather than full retraining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental training after severe heat-related incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed paragraph (h)(4)(iv) requires supplemental training whenever a heat-related injury or illness occurs at the work site that results in death, days away from work, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training could be 'lessons learned' or 'alert' type training and should address deficiencies revealed by the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of employer responsiveness to training questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the training medium does not allow for live Q&A, employers should provide contact information (email or telephone) for someone who can answer questions and are expected to make an effort to respond promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement helps ensure comprehension even when training is asynchronous or remote.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA requests for comment on specific training/standard elements
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA requests comments and evidence on whether it should require other training topics; whether separate training for supervisors/heat safety coordinators is appropriate or if duty-specific training under (h)(1) is sufficient; appropriateness of identified triggers for supplemental training; whether annual refresher training is required or if performance-based supplemental training suffices; and whether OSHA should specify criteria to define start of heat season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are explicit solicitation points for stakeholders to provide evidence and views on possible modifications to the proposed training and timing provisions.
